coreTruths.title: Apical periodontitis is a bacterial disease, so endodontics is fundamentally about controlling infection
coreTruths.broaderContext: Pulpal and periapical disease are bacterial. That single fact shifts the goal of every root canal away from drilling a hole and toward disinfection plus a tight seal.
coreTruths.body:
## The whole point of root canal treatment is bacterial control

The overall aim of endodontic treatment is to prevent or treat periapical periodontitis by controlling infection, which is done by disinfecting the tooth and sealing it well [1]. Conventional root canal treatment is aimed at the treatment and prevention of apical periodontitis through cleaning, shaping, and obturation [2]. Everything else, file choice, irrigation regime, obturation technique, exists to serve that goal.

## Bacteria sit where instruments cannot reach, so chemistry has to do the work

A classic study showed only 50% of teeth treated with hand files and saline alone were free from cultivable bacteria [3]. Mechanical preparation cannot reach every fin, isthmus, and lateral canal in the system. Antibacterial irrigation is required to reach those parts of the root canal system that instruments cannot [4]. That is why sodium hypochlorite, not the file, is doing most of the disinfection.

## Persistent infection has a different microbial signature

Reinfection or persistent infection from missed or inadequately treated canals is the main endodontic cause of failure. The microflora in endodontically treated teeth with persistent infection differs from that of untreated infected teeth, with Enterococcus faecalis and Candida albicans found more frequently in retreatment cases [5]. That shifts the irrigation and medication strategy when retreating, since some organisms resist calcium hydroxide [6].

citations.quote: Infection of the pulp can result in irreversible pulpitis and, if left untreated, periapical periodontitis. The overall aim of endodontic Rx is to prevent or treat periapical periodontitis by controlling infection. This is achieved by disinfecting infected teeth and sealing well thereafter.

Conventional RCT is aimed at the Rx and prevention of apical periodontitis. It involves the cleaning and shaping of the root canal system to remove bacteria and pulpal remnants, followed by obturation of the resultant space to prevent reinfection.
A classic study showed that only 50% of teeth treated with hand files and saline were free from cultivable bacteria.
Therefore, antibacterial irrigation is also required to reach those parts of the root canal system inaccessiblinse to mechanical instrumentation.

Endodontic causes of unfavourable outcome are mainly due to reinfection or persistent infection due to missed or inadequately treated canals. Retreatment involves removal of the original RCF (see …… Removing old root-fillings, p. 355). Microflora in endodontically treated teeth with persistent infection differs from that of untreated, infected teeth; Enterococcus faecalis and Candida albicans are found more frequently in retreatment cases.
These are useful in retreatment cases as certain organisms are resistant to calcium hydroxide.

coreTruths.title: A vital pulp is worth preserving, because it does jobs no restoration can replace
coreTruths.broaderContext: A vital pulp builds dentine, defends against caries, and senses load. Pulp-preserving therapies have the edge over root canals whenever the pulp can still recover.
coreTruths.body:
## A healthy pulp does work that cannot be substituted

The pulp completes root formation, lays down secondary dentine through life, deposits tertiary dentine in response to caries or trauma, maintains sensory function, and keeps dentine elastic [1]. None of that comes back after a root canal, which is why preserving pulp vitality sits at the top of the endodontic hierarchy.

## The pulp-dentine complex can repair itself if given the chance

The pulp-dentine complex is a dynamic connective tissue with inherent repair properties. Removing infected dentine, sealing the cavity, and leaving caries-affected dentine in the depths lets the complex deposit dentine at the advancing front and tertiary dentine at the pulp interface [2]. The cavity does not need to be cleaned to bare pulp to heal.

## Pulp-preserving therapy only works on a pulp that is still salvageable

Indirect or direct pulp protection and pulpotomy are options when caries is close to or exposes the pulp, but only if the pulp is still recoverable. Prerequisites are no symptoms of irreversible pulpitis, a positive response to pulp testing, and no radiographic periapical periodontitis, plus rubber dam and a well-sealed adhesive restoration [3]. Skip those checks and the pulp will fail under the new restoration.

## Calcium silicates have changed what counts as a pulp cap

Direct pulp protection now uses calcium silicate cements such as ProRoot MTA or Biodentine, which aim to prevent bacterial ingress and stimulate a dentine bridge [4]. MTA is biocompatible, sets in moisture, releases calcium hydroxide as it sets, and forms a physical barrier [5]. Discoloration risk from MTA pushed the development of newer biocompatible materials [5]. Stem cell, tissue engineering, and revascularization approaches, grouped as regenerative endodontic procedures, may eventually offer an alternative to root canal treatment in selected cases [6].

citations.quote: A healthy pulp is essential for: Completion of root formation in immature teeth (1° dentine). Continued lifelong tooth development (2° dentine). Protecting against infection when there is loss of enamel/dentine integrity as a result of caries/trauma/tooth surface loss (reactionary and reparative 3° dentine). Maintaining sensory/nociceptive function. Maintaining elasticity of dentine.

Fundamentally, a vital dental pulp and the surrounding dentine (pulp–dentine complex) is a dynamic connective tissue with inherent repair properties. As such, some caries-affected dentine can be left in the depths of a cavity once caries-infected dentine has been removed (see Chapter 6). This removal of the bacteria and their toxins which act as a noxious stimulus and subsequent sealing allows the pulp–dentine complex to deposit dentine at the advancing front of the lesion and reactionary or reparative (3° dentine) at the pulp/dentine interface.

These include no symptoms of irreversible pulpitis, a positive response to pulp testing, and no radiographic evidence of periapical periodontitis. The procedure is carried out under rubber dam isolation and a well-sealed adhesive restoration must be placed.
Direct pulp protection is via calcium silicate cement (e.g. ProRoot® MTA, Biodentine™) the aim being to prevent bacterial ingress following restoration and to stimulate dentine bridge formation.

MTA is a calcium silicate cement, originally developed as a root-end filling material. It is biocompatible and can set in the presence of moisture. It is the material of choice in apexification procedures and can be used as a pulp-capping agent. It creates a physical barrier and releases calcium hydroxide when it is setting. It can be difficult to handle and can cause grey discoloration when used as a root canal filling (RCF) material or pulp-capping agent, this is thought to be due to the presence of bismuth oxide. Other biocompatible products have been developed (ProRoot MTA®, MTA Angelus®, Biodentine®).

In the future, regeneration of pulp and dentine via stem cell therapy, tissue engineering, or revascularization may be an alternative to RCT in selected cases. These procedures are collectively referred to as regenerative endodontic procedures.

coreTruths.title: Disinfection is chemomechanical: shaping serves cleaning, and irrigation is the bigger lever
coreTruths.broaderContext: Files cannot reach every part of a root canal system, so the canal is shaped to let chemistry do the disinfection. Sodium hypochlorite carries most of the load.
coreTruths.body:
## Shape exists to deliver irrigant

The aim of shaping is to remove pulpal debris and microbes and to produce the ideal shape and space for effective penetration of irrigant and resistance form to allow filling [1]. The prepared canal should be a continuously tapering cone from crown to apex that maintains the original anatomy [2]. Shape is not the goal in itself, it is what makes irrigation work.

## Crown-down preparation is about access for chemistry, not just files

Current thinking favours a crown-down approach: prepare the coronal canal first with larger instruments, then work apically with smaller ones [3]. This straightens access, allows better irrigant flow, and reduces apical extrusion of infected debris because most bacteria sit in the coronal region of an infected canal [4]. Apical preparation should be at least ISO size 25 to allow adequate irrigation [5].

## Sodium hypochlorite is the gold standard, but only if it is exchanged often

Sodium hypochlorite is bactericidal and dissolves organic debris, often used at 2.5% [6]. It must not be extruded beyond the apex because it causes inflammation and tissue necrosis; a side-vented needle 2-3 mm short of working length reduces extrusion risk [6]. Frequent exchange and flooding of the canal matters, it lowers torsional forces on files and aids disinfection [6].

## EDTA cleans up what hypochlorite cannot

Instrumentation produces a smear layer. EDTA is a calcium ion chelating agent that dissolves the inorganic component of the smear layer, which sodium hypochlorite cannot, so EDTA is used after instrumentation followed by a final rinse of sodium hypochlorite [7]. Combining the two does what neither does alone.

## Apical anatomy sets the working length

Apical foramina usually sit 0.5-0.7 mm away from the anatomical and radiographic apex, and the apical constriction lies 0.5-0.7 mm short of the foramina, with both distances increasing with age due to secondary cementum [8]. Working length should be set 1-2 mm from the radiographic apex, and an electronic apex locator should be used alongside radiographs [8]. On lower 5s and 7s, prepare 1 mm from the zero reading because of the IDN [9].

citations.quote: The aims of shaping are to remove pulpal debris and microbes and produce the ideal shape and space for effective penetration of irrigant and the resistance form to allow filling of the space with root filling material.

The prepared canal should be a continuously tapering cone from crown to apex and should maintain the original anatomy. The apical constriction and original canal length should be maintained as far as possible.

Current thinking favours the development of shape in a crown-down manner. Many single-file systems are in use now and the techniques recommended by each manufacturer vary. When using a progressive sequence of files, preparation of the coronal part of the canal is done first with larger instruments. Then the root canal is prepared with progressively smaller instruments.

↓ the likelihood of apical extrusion of infected material as most of the canal debris is removed before apical instrumentation takes place. Important because the majority of bacteria in an infected root canal are located in the coronal region.
Generally, apical preparation should be at least ISO size 25 to facilitate adequate irrigation.

Sodium hypochlorite is the gold standard. It is an effective irrigant as it is both bactericidal and dissolves organic debris. There is some controversy over the appropriate concentration. The higher-concentration solutions have been shown to dissolve tissue at a quicker rate. Sodium hypochlorite is available in many different concentrations and it is often used at 2.5%. It should not be extruded beyond the apex as it can cause inflammation and tissue necrosis. The use of a side vented needle 2–3mm short of working length reduces the risk of sodium hypochlorite extrusion.

Instrumentation of the root canal wall produces a smear layer. EDTA is a calcium ion chelating agent which dissolves the inorganic component of the smear layer which sodium hypochlorite cannot do, as it only dissolves the organic tissue. EDTA solution can be used after instrumentation is complete followed by a final rinse of sodium hypochlorite.

The apical foramina are usually sited 0.5–0.7mm away from the anatomical and radiographic apex. The apical constriction usually occurs 0.5–0.7mm short of the foramina. These distances ↑ with age due to deposition of 2° cementum. Root filling to the constriction provides a natural stop to instrumentation, thus the working length should be established 1–2mm from the radiographic apex. Electronic apex locators are frequently used to assess the approximate position of the apical constriction and should be used in conjunction with radiographs to optimize the working length.
It is advisable to prepare 1mm from the zero reading of an apex locator on lower 5s and 7s as the apices are potentially very close to the inferior dental nerve (IDN).

coreTruths.title: Coronal seal is as important as the root filling, and the final restoration is part of the endodontics
coreTruths.broaderContext: A perfectly obturated canal still fails if the crown leaks. Coronal seal and definitive restoration are not the next appointment's problem, they are part of treatment.
coreTruths.body:
## Obturation needs both an apical and a coronal seal

Obturation aims to incarcerate residual bacteria, prevent reinfection, prevent ingress of inflammatory exudate (apical seal), and prevent bacteria and tissue fluid from entering the system (coronal seal) [1]. Both seals matter, leakage from either end means failure.

## A poor coronal restoration sinks good endodontics

After obturation, an ideal restorative material on the pulp chamber floor and orifices plus a definitive restoration is required to achieve a good coronal seal. This is now recognised as very important for success in endodontics, and too often good endodontic therapy is jeopardised by a poor restoration that does not provide a good coronal seal [2]. Quality of the coronal restoration sits alongside quality of root filling and pre-treatment periapical status as one of the three main prognostic factors [3].

## Definitive restoration cannot wait

Definitive restoration needs to be carried out as soon as possible. The longer a provisional restoration sits, the higher the risk of coronal leakage and fracture [4]. If there is a delay, molar provisionals should still have cuspal coverage [5].

## Root-treated teeth need protection, not just filling

Root-treated teeth are weakened by loss of tooth substance from the original cavity, restoration, and access, by dehydration, and by loss of dentine elasticity from irrigants and medicaments on collagen [6]. Cuspal coverage for root-treated molars enhances survival, and a ferrule effect (an extracoronal restoration surrounding a 2 mm collar of dentine coronal to the preparation margin) is the structural target [7]. Anterior root-treated teeth do not need crowning unless there has been substantial loss of structure [8]. Adhesive onlays or partial coverage crowns can deliver cuspal protection without the tissue loss of a full crown [9].

citations.quote: To provide a 3-D hermetic seal to the root canal to: Prevent the ingress of bacteria or tissue fluids which might act as a culture medium for any bacteria that remain in the root canal system. Called a coronal seal. Incarcerate any microbes remaining in the root canal system. Prevent reinfection of the root canal system. Prevent diffusion of inflammatory exudate into the canal, called an apical seal.

After completing obturation, a good coronal seal must be achieved by placement of an ideal restorative material on the pulp chamber floor and canal orifices and placement of a definitive restoration. This is now recognized as very important for success in endodontics. Too often good endodontic therapy is jeopardized by a poor restoration that does not provide a good coronal seal.

Three main prognostic factors influence the outcome: Pre-treatment status of the periapical tissues—if there is no pre-treatment radiolucency, outcome is more favourable and can be up to 95%. If there is a lesion, outcome is more favourable for smaller (<5mm) lesions. Quality and length of RCF—outcome is more favourable if well compacted and reaches within 2mm of the radiographic apex. Quality of coronal restoration.
Definitive restoration needs to be carried out as soon as possible. The longer a provisional restoration is in place the higher the risk of coronal leakage and #.
If there is a delay in placement of the final restoration (e.g. awaiting resolution of sinus tract) then molar restorations should have cuspal coverage in the temporary restoration.

Protection of remaining tooth structure—root-treated teeth are substantially weakened by: Loss of tooth substance as a result of the original cavity/restoration and also by subsequent access cavity and root canal preparation. Dehydration. Loss of elasticity of dentine due to effect of irrigants and medicaments on collagen.

Cuspal coverage for root-treated molar teeth enhances survival. The success of this restoration will depend on how much sound coronal tooth substance remains and whether a ‘ferrule effect’ can be achieved, i.e. an extra-coronal restoration surrounds a ‘collar’ of dentine of at least 2mm height coronal to the preparation margins.
Anterior root-treated teeth do not require crowning unless there has been substantial loss of tooth structure.

Use of adhesive materials where possible allows for preservation of tooth tissue. Where cuspal protection is needed, onlays or partial coverage crowns can provide the necessary occlusal form without excessive tooth tissue loss which would result from full crown preparation.

coreTruths.title: Endodontic outcome is judged by tooth survival, not by a binary success or failure
coreTruths.broaderContext: Endodontic outcome data is moving away from success or failure toward tooth survival, the same yardstick used for implants. That changes how clinicians review and counsel.
coreTruths.body:
## Survival, not success, is the modern frame

Success and failure as terms have given way to a more pragmatic view: an asymptomatic functional tooth with a reduction in any apical area is acceptable. Calling that tooth survival lines endodontics up with the criteria used for implants [1].

## Three prognostic factors carry most of the weight

Pre-treatment periapical status, quality and length of root filling, and quality of coronal restoration are the three main prognostic factors. With no pre-treatment radiolucency, outcomes can reach up to 95%; smaller lesions (<5 mm) do better than larger ones; root fillings do better when well compacted and within 2 mm of the radiographic apex [2]. Patients should be counselled accordingly.

## Outcomes get described in three categories, with a 4-year window for the uncertain ones

Favourable means symptom free, functional, healthy clinical and radiographic tissues, or healing by scar [3]. Uncertain covers low-grade tenderness or persistent radiolucency within the 4-year assessment period [4]. Unfavourable covers symptoms, non-functional teeth, sinus tracts, or new or persisting radiolucency [5]. Conventionally a decision is made at 1 year, with up to 4 years of follow-up for uncertain cases [6].

## CBCT is for the cases that conventional films do not solve

CBCT is indicated where there are symptoms but conventional radiography shows no radiolucency, or where missed canal anatomy is suspected [7]. It is a problem-solving tool, not a routine review film.

## Single versus multi-visit does not change radiological outcome

There is no evidence that single- or multiple-visit RCT is more effective in terms of radiological success, although single-visit may slightly increase the frequency of swelling and need for analgesics [8]. Pre-treatment symptoms or swelling, complex anatomy, or patient management factors drive the choice; it is not a quality marker.

citations.quote: Previously, the terms ‘success and ‘failure’ were used. It may be more pragmatic to consider that the absence of clinical signs and symptoms and a ↓ in size of any apical area be deemed acceptable. Considering this as tooth survival (having an asymptomatic functional tooth) is more in line with the criteria used to judge the outcome of implant placement.

Three main prognostic factors influence the outcome: Pre-treatment status of the periapical tissues—if there is no pre-treatment radiolucency, outcome is more favourable and can be up to 95%. If there is a lesion, outcome is more favourable for smaller (<5mm) lesions. Quality and length of RCF—outcome is more favourable if well compacted and reaches within 2mm of the radiographic apex. Quality of coronal restoration.
Symptom free, functional tooth, clinical healthy tissues, radiographic evidence of healthy periapical tissues or healing by scar tissue formation.
Symptoms or symptom free. May be low-grade tenderness to palpation/percussion. Radiographically, periapical radiolucency persists within the 4yr assessment period.
Presence of symptoms, tooth not functional, clinical signs of infection, e.g. sinus tract/swelling. Radiographically, a new radiolucency or radiolucency has persisted or ↑ in size.

Conventionally, 1yr is considered the time at which a decision on outcome can be made. If there are symptoms, the patient may be reviewed sooner. If the outcome is uncertain, follow-up for a total of 4yrs is needed.
CBCT may be indicated where there are symptoms but conventional radiography shows no radiolucency or where missed canal anatomy may be suspected.

There is no evidence that single- or multiple-visit RCT is more effective, in terms of radiological success. Single-visit RCT may result in a slightly ↑ frequency of swelling and ↑ need of analgesics.
